newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr makes tentative rise, rates a worry.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr makes tentative rise, rates a worry.

text.p: The Australian dollar crept cautiously higher Wednesday helped by a bounce in US$/yen, although a late scare over Japanese rates capped gains.

Bulls were also heartened by the Federal Reserve's decision not to raise U.S. rates and by a firm set of domestic wages data, all of which suggested the A$ may keep its yield advantage over the U.S. currency for a while yet.

The main risk to the steadier tone were final data on Australian average weekly earnings out on Thursday which could yet see easing speculation reborn if private sector pay deals are as subdued as some suspect.
By 4.40 pm (0640 GMT) the dollar had inched up to US$0.7761/66 from an early US$0.7734/39 and a US$0.7713 low offshore. It finished here Tuesday at US$0.7741/46.
Traders said bids from corporates and local banks had established the resilience of support beneath US$0.7720 and caught much of the market in a short squeeze.
The drift upwards was encouraged by an early bounce in US$/yen, although gains were pared when a Bank of Japan official said the bank was considering the right timing for a rate rise.
The comment sent Japanese shares tumbling and bond yields surging and pulled the U.S. dollar back to 113.40 from 114.00.
The A$ flinched to 88.15/25 from 88.80 but was still up on Tuesday's 87.10/20. The trade weighted index was steady at 58.6.
The Fed's decision not to raise U.S. rates was seen as a mixed blessing for the local dollar.
On one hand it kept the A$'s modest yield advantage intact for the moment, but some reckoned it also provided a window of opportunity for the Reserve Bank to cut rates here.

The easing argument mainly hinged on the belief the recent wages growth which so alarmed the RBA, had been biased upward by special circumstances in the public sector and private deals were much more subdued.

Some expected proof of this to be provided by final average weekly earnings data on Thursday and were inclined to dismiss today's wages survey as unrepresentative of the general trend, noting it covered less than three percent of all employees.

The Department of Industrial Relations data on enterprise bargains showed average annualised growth in the private sector rose to 4.8 percent in the March quarter from 4.4 percent in Q4. In all sectors it rose to 4.7 percent from 4.4 percent.
Analysts, especially those in the easing camp, cautioned the data covered only a tiny percentage of the workforce and weekly earnings data would be far more important for the rate outlook.

Those looking for steady policy noted the RBA did look at the DIR data and it had to be worrying that private sector deals had accelerated while unemployment was still around 8.5 percent. "The report showed wages growth remains strong, reducing the chances of a near term rate cut by the RBA," said Nomura economist Andrew Pease. "It appears wage negotiators have not yet adjusted to a low inflation enviroment."
This opinion was echoed by Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith who said wage increases were too high for Australia's current low inflation environment.
Neither did it look like growth would slow anytime soon.

"The prospects for an easing in the pace of wages growth are not positive" said Nomura's Pease, noting press reports suggested the big banking unions were planning to ask for a seven percent rise this year.
But the rate cut talk might yet grow if the final figures on Q1 average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) confirm suspicions private sector growth had not accelerated sharply.

The initial data showed a surprisingly strong rise in overall wages to an annual 4.6 percent from 3.9 percent in Q3, but analysts see a good chance annual growth in private deals will be under 3.5 percent. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
